candidates.title: Effectiveness of Constrained-Generation Plus Formal Verification for Preventing Unsafe Network Changes
candidates.research_question: Does a pipeline combining grammar-constrained LLM decoding with formal verification and emulation execution reduce unsafe network-change proposals compared with unconstrained LLM generation?
hypotheses: H1: Constrained-generation + formal verification yields a lower proportion of unsafe configs (that would violate specified safety properties) than unconstrained LLM outputs.
H2: A non-negligible fraction of unsafe configs remain undetected by the formal verifier (false negatives) and are caught only by emulation execution.
candidates.proposed_design: Paired experimental design. Use a public/synthetic set of high-level intents -> target-config tasks (multiple vendors simulated). For each intent, produce two outputs from the same LLM seed: (A) unconstrained generation, (B) grammar-constrained generation. Feed both into a formal verifier (reachability/policy checks). Execute both passing and verifier-failed configs in Mininet emulation to observe runtime safety violations. Measure per-intent unsafe rates at three checkpoints: raw output, post-verifier, post-emulation/rollback.
candidates.expected_data: Per-intent binary labels for violation at raw output, verification pass/fail, and emulation-observed violation; counts and timestamps; per-model prompt and seed; verifier error logs.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in unsafe-change rate (proportion) at the verification checkpoint and residual unsafe rate after emulation between constrained and unconstrained conditions.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute paired proportions and differences; McNemar's test for paired binary outcomes; estimate 95% CIs for reduction; analyze false-negative rate of verifier (configs flagged safe but failing emulation); stratify by vendor/command-category.
risks: Formal verifier may not model vendor-specific semantics causing inflated false-negative/positive rates.
Emulation (Mininet) may not reproduce certain device behaviors, limiting external validity.
Prompt sensitivity may cause results to depend on prompting idiosyncrasies.

candidates.title: Convergence and Efficiency of Iterative Self-Critique and Repair for Network-Config Generation
candidates.research_question: Do bounded iterative self-critique and repair loops reliably converge to correct, verifier-approved network configurations within practical iteration limits for typical NetOps intents?
hypotheses: H1: Iterative repair with verifier feedback increases verifier-approved configs relative to single-shot generation.
H2: Most convergent cases succeed within a small number of iterations (e.g., <=5); a long tail of nonconvergent cases exists for complex intents.
candidates.proposed_design: Select a representative intent set. For each intent, generate initial config; run up to K repair iterations where the LLM ingests verifier counterexamples/error messages and attempts repair. Stop on verifier approval or K iterations. Record iteration-to-success, total model calls, and final emulation outcome.
candidates.expected_data: Iteration counts per intent, verifier decision per iteration, intermediate generated configs, emulation outcomes, failure-mode annotations.
candidates.primary_outcome: Convergence rate within K iterations and distribution of iterations-to-success; proportion of verifier-approved configs that still fail in emulation.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate Kaplan–Meier-like survival curve (iterations-to-success); report median iterations among successes; logistic regression to predict convergence from intent complexity; compute proportion of verifier-approved-but-failing emulation cases.
risks: Repair iterations may exploit prompt artifacts (overfitting to verifier messages) rather than genuinely correcting semantics.
Verifier feedback may be uninformative for LLM-driven repair, causing nonconvergence.
Compute budget and API rate limits if iterations per intent are large.

candidates.title: Adversarial Intent and Plausible-but-Unsafe Config Generation: Evaluating Verifier Robustness
candidates.research_question: How susceptible are grammar-constrained + verifier pipelines to adversarial or malformed intents that elicit plausible-but-unsafe configurations that evade automated checks?
hypotheses: H1: Adversarially-crafted intents can significantly increase the rate of unsafe configs that pass the verifier (escape rate) compared with benign intents.
H2: Increasing verifier strictness and constrained-decoding reduces escape rate but may increase false positives (blocking safe changes).
candidates.proposed_design: Create adversarial-intent mutations (lexical ambiguity, negation flips, vendor-specific synonyms, crafted prompts) from benign intents. For each intent variant, run constrained-generation + verifier pipeline and measure whether unsafe configs are produced and whether the verifier flags them. Vary verifier rule-sets (strict/medium/lenient).
candidates.expected_data: Per-intent-variant labels: unsafe_by_emulation (yes/no), verifier_flag (pass/fail), mutation type, model outputs.
candidates.primary_outcome: Escape rate: proportion of adversarial variants producing unsafe configs that pass verifier; escape-rate difference vs benign baseline.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare escape rates using exact binomial tests; model escape probability as function of mutation type and verifier strictness; report CI and effect sizes.
risks: Adversarial mutation generation may be heuristic and not fully representative of real attacker behavior.
Ethical considerations: must avoid releasing exploit patterns that enable unsafe production misuse.
High verifier strictness settings may produce impractically high false-positive rejection rates.

candidates.title: Quantifying Operator Burden vs. Residual Risk for Staged Human-in-the-Loop Approval Protocols
candidates.research_question: What is the trade-off between operator time/burden and residual unsafe-change probability under different human-in-loop approval policies in an LLM-driven NetOps pipeline?
hypotheses: H1: Selective human review (e.g., review only verifier-failed or sampled outputs) achieves most risk reduction of full-review at substantially lower operator time.
H2: Blind or no-review policies yield unacceptably high residual unsafe-change probabilities for moderate-complexity intents.
candidates.proposed_design: Simulate three approval policies on same generated outputs: (1) full human review, (2) verifier-gated review (only verifier-failed cases reviewed), (3) sampled review (random p%). Use time-per-review estimates from literature or operator-survey proxies; compute residual unsafe-change probability after each policy using emulation labels.
candidates.expected_data: Per-policy: operator-hours, number of reviews, residual unsafe-change proportion, latency metrics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Pareto frontier: operator time (hours) vs residual unsafe-change probability; identification of diminishing-returns regions.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute expected operator-time per intent; compare residual risk across policies with bootstrap CIs; sensitivity analysis over review time assumptions.
risks: Operator time estimates may be imprecise without field measurements.
Simulated operator decisions (binary accept/reject) may not capture real cognitive processes or partial fixes.
Ethical/operational acceptability of policies depends on organization risk tolerance, limiting generalizability.

candidates.title: NetOps Safety Testbed and Baseline Benchmark: Integrated Generation→Verify→Execute Metrics and Public Dataset Release
candidates.research_question: Can a compact, public NetOps safety testbed combining intent-to-config tasks, formal verification checks, emulation execution, and rollback metrics provide reproducible baseline measurements and expose common failure modes of LLM-driven NetOps pipelines?
hypotheses: H1: An integrated testbed and dataset will reveal baseline unsafe-change rates for common LLM prompting strategies and serve as a reproducible benchmark.
H2: Baseline experiments will identify a small set of recurrent failure patterns (vendor-syntax errors, missing state assumptions, security-policy violations).
candidates.proposed_design: Construct a proof-of-concept testbed: curated intent set (multi-vendor synthetic + annotated), verification rule-set (reachability and policy), Mininet scenarios for execution, and metrics (raw unsafe rate, post-verifier residual, emulation rollback cost, operator-review effort). Run selected LLM prompting baselines and report benchmark results; publish dataset and evaluation scripts.
candidates.expected_data: Released dataset (intents, reference configs, vendor labels), evaluation scripts, baseline model outputs, verifier logs, emulation traces, metric summaries.
candidates.primary_outcome: Availability of the benchmark and baseline numeric results (unsafe rates at each pipeline stage) enabling future comparisons.
candidates.analysis_outline: Report descriptive baseline metrics; categorize failure modes with frequency counts; provide reproducible scripts and instructions; include guidance on metric interpretation.
risks: Dataset may not capture real-world vendor heterogeneity at production scale.
Risk of inadvertently releasing sensitive command templates — must ensure all artifacts are synthetic or sanitized.
Maintaining and curating benchmark over time requires resources beyond initial release.
